title: Virtual care that works for patients, caregivers and clinicians
title_html: Virtual care that works for patients, caregivers and clinicians
hook: A virtual-care platform rebuilt around patients over 60 — and the daughters, sons and clinicians around them.
dek: Fourteen months on a virtual-care platform for patients over 60. Helpers got their own keys, joining became one tap, and intake started speaking plain English.
team: Designers, a researcher, a PM, engineers and clinical advisors

tldr: Older patients were the platform’s heaviest users, and every missed video visit cost a clinic slot.
I led design for delegated caregiver access, Today-first booking and one-tap joining with an audio fallback.
We killed a symptom-checker chatbot and gave that load to clinicians.

challenge.inherited: “My daughter books everything, so I just give her my password,” one patient told us in our first round of interviews.
challenge.body: The platform served a network of family practices, and most of its video patients were over 60. Helpers signed in with their parents’ passwords, intake asked for the same history at every visit, and one in five video visits started late or not at all. Each workaround cost the clinic a visit and the patient some dignity.

role_led: Designed the patient app, caregiver access and the clinician request queue, end to end
Planned two usability rounds with our researcher: 12 patients aged 60+ each, on their own phones
Wrote the plain-language standard and rewrote intake with our clinical advisors
Mapped every flow to WCAG 2.2 AA and reviewed builds with engineering every sprint
Framed each decision for the client’s medical lead and product owner, trade-offs first
role_team: Our researcher recruited through the clinics and ran a two-week diary study with 15 caregivers
Another designer owned the clinician desktop and the shared component library
Our clinical advisors, a family physician and a nurse, wrote and checked every routing rule
Our engineers shipped iOS, Android and web from one set of components
constraints: Health-privacy law and clinic consent policy
Express, revocable consent for every helper

principles.title: Never make someone prove who they are twice.
principles.body: A passkey or a one-time email link, a helper’s own sign-in, and intake that remembers. Every repeated question is a chance to give up.

principles.title: The safest path is the obvious one.
principles.body: If video is wrong for the problem, the screen says so and offers the next safe step: in person, a nurse line or emergency services.

principles.title: Plain language is a clinical requirement.
principles.body: A patient who misreads a question answers it wrongly. Every screen reads at grade 8 or lower (SMOG), and a clinician signs off the words.

decisions.decision: Delegated caregiver access, scoped, expiring and audited, replaces password-sharing
decisions.why: In the diary study, 11 of 15 caregivers signed in with their parent’s password. The clinic could not tell who had agreed to what.
decisions.tradeoff: Inviting a helper adds two screens, and every permission has to explain itself in one line.
decisions.risk: Patients granting more than they mean to. Defaults are the narrowest useful set, and visit notes start off.
decisions.owner: Me, with the PM and the client’s privacy officer

decisions.decision: Booking leads with Today / Tomorrow / This week, from lead-time data
decisions.why: 55% of visits were booked for today or tomorrow, yet booking opened on a month calendar.
decisions.tradeoff: Patients planning weeks ahead take one extra tap to reach the calendar.
decisions.risk: Days with no same-day capacity. An empty Today says so and offers a call to the clinic.
decisions.owner: Me, with the PM and the clinic schedulers

decisions.decision: One-tap join with a device check and an audio-only fallback
decisions.why: Most late or missed starts came from camera permissions and weak connections.
decisions.tradeoff: Some visits begin without video, so the visit record notes the mode.
decisions.risk: Audio being used where the clinician needs to see the patient. Clinicians can ask for video with one tap.
decisions.owner: Me and the mobile engineering lead

decisions.decision: An appropriateness screen that routes plainly to in-person care, a nurse line or emergency services
decisions.why: Some problems should never be a video visit. Patients needed to hear that while booking, before a doctor said it two minutes into a call.
decisions.tradeoff: Everyone sees one more screen before booking, so it is one question with three plain answers.
decisions.risk: Under-triage: someone with chest pain booking a video visit anyway. The emergency answer is a full-width call button, the request records the answer chosen, and the clinical advisors reviewed routed cases every month.
decisions.owner: Clinical advisors for the content, me for the flow

decisions.decision: A clinician approval step for prescription renewals
decisions.why: About a third of bookings were renewals. A two-minute review settled many of them, or chose the right kind of visit.
decisions.tradeoff: Patients wait up to one working day for an answer instead of booking straight away.
decisions.risk: Requests going stale. The queue shows waiting time, and anything older than a day rises to the top.
decisions.owner: Me and our other designer, with the clinical advisors

decisions.why: It was in the original brief. With no automated diagnosis allowed, it could only guess, and a wrong guess here is a safety incident, not a bug.
decisions.tradeoff: We dropped a feature the client had already promised its board. Triage stayed with people.
decisions.risk: Clinician workload. The approval step and the appropriateness screen took the load the chatbot was meant to carry.
decisions.owner: Me, with the clinical advisors and the client’s medical lead

process.heading: Give the helper their own key
body: Daughters and sons were already doing the booking and the joining, signed in with their parents’ passwords. So we made the helper a real person in the system: invited by name, with their own sign-in, a short list of things they can do, and an end date.
Both people see the same log of what the helper did. That one screen made the client’s privacy officer comfortable, and it was the screen patients tapped most in testing.

figure.caption: D1 · Delegated access: invited by name, scoped, expiring, and logged for both people.

process.heading: Lead with today
body: Six months of booking data showed what the month calendar was hiding: most people wanted to be seen today or tomorrow, and almost nobody planned two weeks out.
Booking now opens on Today, with Tomorrow and This week one tap away, and each slot names the doctor and whether it is video or phone.

figure.caption: D2 · Booking leads with Today / Tomorrow / This week.

process.heading: A way in when video fails
body: The device check runs before the doctor is waiting. On a weak connection we start with audio and say so in one sentence, with the video button the biggest thing on the call screen.
Before booking, one question asks whether video is right at all. Chest pain goes to emergency services, uncertainty to a nurse line, and hands-on problems to an in-person visit.

figure.caption: D3 · Audio first on a weak connection; video stays one tap away.

process.heading: Criteria that changed screens
body: We treated WCAG 2.2 AA as design input from the first sketch. Five of the newer criteria changed screens outright: how people sign in, what intake asks, where help lives, how big targets are, and what the sticky Join bar may cover.

figure.caption: Each criterion maps to a decision we can point at on screen.

compare.caption: Intake asks what changed and confirms the medicines on file. SMOG 15 → 8, median 11 → 4 min.

system.heading: A care kit for older eyes and unsteady hands
system.body: One accent, an amber that routes without alarming, and type that never drops below 19 px in the patient app.

colors.use: Primary actions, Join, links · 5.97 : 1 with white
Warm off-white background, less glare than pure white
Routing to emergency services, a nurse line or in person · amber, never alarm red

artifacts.caption: Five criteria that changed what we drew.

head: WCAG 2.2 criterion
Design decision
rows: Passkey or a one-time email link; no puzzles, no memorized passwords
Intake prefilled from the profile and last visit; confirm instead of retype
“Call the clinic” in the same place on every screen
The sticky Join bar never covers a focused field (scroll padding)

after_launch.what: Join works across iOS, Android and web; about one visit in nine starts on audio
Helpers invited by name instead of borrowing passwords
Fewer missed video visits; caregiver-linked accounts reach 21%

not_taken: One shared login with a PIN to switch between patient and helper. Faster to build, but consent and the audit log would have been fiction.
A smarter month calendar. The lead-time data said people think in days, not dates.
An SMS-only join for older phones. We kept text reminders and sent everyone to the same one-tap join.
reflections: Plain language took more clinical review time than any single screen. Next time I would plan for it from the first week instead of treating it as copy polish.
Remote sessions on people’s own phones and Wi-Fi found more problems than any lab session. Most of what we fixed in joining came from them.

deeper.title: How helper consent works
body: The patient invites a helper by name and mobile number. The helper gets a text with a link and sets up their own sign-in, a passkey or a one-time email link, never the patient’s password.
Each permission is its own switch with a one-line explanation, and visit notes start off. Access ends on a date the patient picks, 90 days by default, and both people get a reminder a week before.
Clinicians see who acted: “Booked by Lena O. for Marguerite O.” That line, and the shared log, is what the privacy impact assessment signed off on.

deeper.title: The appropriateness screen
body: One question before booking: is a video visit right for this? Three plain answers, written and reviewed by our clinical advisors: chest pain or trouble breathing, call emergency services now; not sure, call the nurse line; needs a hands-on exam, book in person.

Urgent routing uses amber, never alarm red: in testing, red read as an error the patient had made. The urgency is in the words and the size: the emergency answer is a full-width “Call emergency services” button.

deeper.title: How we measured it
body: No-shows: video visits in the six months after launch against the six months before, same clinics.
Intake time: median from the first intake screen to submit, from product analytics. SUS: two rounds of 12 patients aged 60 and over, tested on their own phones.

privacy_note: Names and details changed to protect patient privacy.
